title: Working Scientifically
seo_title: Year 6 Science: Working Scientifically Worksheets (Fair Tests, Variables, Graphs)
standard_text: Plan different types of scientific enquiries to answer questions, including recognising and controlling variables where necessary; take measurements with increasing accuracy and precision, taking repeat readings when appropriate; record data and results using tables, bar and line graphs and scatter graphs; use test results to make predictions; report and present findings, including conclusions; identify scientific evidence that has been used to support or refute ideas.
meta_desc: Free Year 6 science worksheets on working scientifically: fair tests, variables, repeat readings, anomalous results, choosing graphs, predictions and conclusions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Change one thing, measure one thing.
key_sub: Keep the rest the same, repeat readings, and let the evidence decide.
body_html:
How to think about it

Plan a fair test, measure carefully, then let the results answer the question.

  • Change one variable, measure one variable, keep everything else the same.
  • Repeat readings; spot anomalous results; find the mean of the good ones.
  • Bar chart for groups, line graph for change over time, scatter graph for a link between two measurements. Conclusions must match the evidence.
Example

Results 14, 15, 26, 16. Anomaly and mean?

26 does not fit

(14 + 15 + 16) ÷ 3

Answer: 26 is anomalous; mean = 15

Example

Plant height every week: which graph?

Change over time

Answer: a line graph

Common mistakes

  • Changing two variables at once.
  • Including an anomalous result in the mean.
  • Using a line graph for separate groups.

faq.q: What are the three kinds of variable?
faq.a: The variable you change, the variable you measure, and the variables you keep the same (control variables) to make the test fair.
Repeats show whether results agree. They help you spot anomalous results and give a more reliable mean.
A bar chart for separate groups, a line graph for something that changes over time or along a scale, and a scatter graph to see if two measurements are linked.

items.q: Investigation: "Does the temperature of water affect how fast sugar dissolves?" Which variable should be changed?
c: the same amount of sugar and water, and stirring the same way
the time for the sugar to dissolve
items.e: Change one variable: the one in the question.

items.q: Investigation: "Does the type of soil affect how much water drains through it?" What should be kept the same to make it a fair test?
c: the same amount of soil, the same amount of water and the same funnel
the volume of water that drains through in 5 minutes
items.e: Control variables keep the test fair.

items.q: Investigation: "Does the length of a paper helicopter's wings affect how long it takes to fall?" Which variable should be changed?
c: the same paper, the same drop height and the same paperclip
items.e: Change one variable: the one in the question.

items.q: Investigation: "Does the type of soil affect how much water drains through it?" What should be measured?
c: the same amount of soil, the same amount of water and the same funnel
the volume of water that drains through in 5 minutes
items.e: Measure the result (the dependent variable).

items.q: Why do scientists repeat measurements?
c: to check results and make them more reliable
because the first result is always wrong
items.e: Repeats show if results agree.

items.q: What should you do with an anomalous result?
c: repeat the test or leave it out of the mean
items.e: It may be a mistake.

the force needed to pull the shoe

items.q: What is a fair test?
c: a test where only one variable is changed and the others are kept the same
items.e: Change one thing.

items.q: Which equipment measures force?
items.e: Force is measured in newtons.

items.q: Which equipment measures time accurately?
items.e: Time in seconds.

c: the same type of seed, soil and amount of water
the height of the plant after two weeks
items.e: Measure the result (the dependent variable).

items.q: What is a prediction?
c: what you think will happen, with a reason
items.e: Made before the test.

items.q: Investigation: "Does the type of surface affect how much force is needed to pull a shoe?" What should be kept the same to make it a fair test?

items.q: Investigation: "Does the length of a paper helicopter's wings affect how long it takes to fall?" What should be measured?

items.q: What is a conclusion?
c: what the results show, answering the question
items.e: Based on evidence.

items.q: What is an anomalous result?
c: a result that does not fit the pattern of the others
items.e: Check it or repeat it.
